title: Stabilizing Extrapolation in Looped Transformers via Learned Stochastic Stopping
claim: Fixed-depth models fail abruptly out of distribution with high run-to-run variance, while learned stochastic stopping gives smoother, more consistent extrapolation.
layout: 4 panels in a row, shared axes, shaded ID/OOD regions, dashed per-length maximum
description: Four side-by-side line plots share a y-axis (accuracy 0–1) and an x-axis (number of digits, 5–60). The panels are titled Transformers, Looped (K=20), Looped (K=#digits) and Looped (RL-Halting). A dashed vertical line near 20 digits splits each panel into a blue-tinted ID (train) region and a red-tinted OOD region. Each panel has thin translucent lines for individual runs, a bold line for the mean and a dashed line for the per-length maximum. The Transformers panel (blue and red, L=3 and L=60) drops sharply to 0 right after the training length, with the runs tightly bunched. The orange K=20 and green K=#digits panels fan out widely across runs, and their mean curves sit far below the dashed maxima. The purple RL-Halting panel has tightly clustered runs and a mean close to its maximum. The eye goes first to the spread of thin lines in the middle panels.
caption: Oracle-over-iterations accuracy on binary addition as a function of input length for standard Transformers and Looped Transformers with fixed K = 20, length-matched K = n, and RL-Halting. RL-Halting is shown for reference and discussed in § 4.3. The shaded region marks the training-length regime (ID), and the right-hand side corresponds to longer OOD inputs. Thin solid lines denote individual runs, the bold solid line denotes the mean across runs, and the dashed line denotes the per-length maximum across runs.
abstract: Looped Transformers, which repeatedly apply a shared transformer block, are an architecturally natural fit for variable-length algorithmic tasks. Although they can exhibit strong length generalization beyond the length of training sequences, this behavior is brittle, yielding high out-of-distribution (OOD) variance, even across well-performing in-distribution solutions. We trace this variance to the spurious correlation in simple algorithmic tasks between sequence length and number of loops. Introducing stochasticity into the number of loops during training sharply reduces OOD variance and stabilizes predictions across inference-time loop counts. To improve upon heuristic randomization schemes, we further analyze RL-Halting as a learned stochastic schedule and find that it generally improves the accuracy-stability trade-off. Across binary addition, Dyck-1, Unique Set, and Copy, learned stochastic stopping often improves this trade-off but can also stabilize a suboptimal computation. Our work suggests that "when to stop" should be treated as a training-time design choice, not merely an inference-time computation-allocation rule.
